newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: FEATURE - Like sleeping in a tea factory? Try Sri Lanka.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Like sleeping in a tea factory? Try Sri Lanka.

text.p: Want to sleep in an old tea withering loft? Get a welcome drink in the drier room and sip your whisky in the tea packing area?
Spend a night at the "Tea Factory", the latest of Sri Lanka's concept hotels and you'll get to do all these.
It's turning out to be everyone's cup of tea. You wake up to a breathtaking view of miles of lush green tea bushes and blue hills, which makes it hard to believe that you are in tropical Sri Lanka.

But the Tea Factory at Kandapola's Hethersett Estate, situated at 6,800 feet (2,100 metres) above sea level, is as much a part of Sri Lanka as the sweltering capital Colombo and pristine white beaches in the eastern port city of Trincomalee.
The road to the hotel is not every driver's delight, but once you get to the Tea Factory the journey over gravel, dirt and bumps from the central hill city of Nuwara Eliya is worth the effort.
"Most hotels are becoming monotonous. They look the same. This is different," said R. Sridharan, the hotel's acting manager.
"Sleeping in a tea withering loft is appreciated by people," he said.
HOTEL WITH A CHEQUERED HISTORY
Time stopped at the Hethersett tea factory for 21 years after it was shut down in 1973 following nationalisation of private tea estates.
But until its closure, the factory played an important role in the development of Sri Lanka's tea industry and in helping Ceylon Tea become one of the world's favourite beverages.
A historical account of the Hethersett Estate shows the land was bought in the 1870s by one W. Flowerdew, who was the first planter-proprietor, agent and resident manager.
He apparently named the estate after a village southwest of Norwich in England, from where he probably came. But Flowerdew sold the plantation in 1881 and went back home.
In 1891, Hethersett tea fetched a record price for silver tip tea from Ceylon. A pound was auctioned in Mincing Lane, London, for more than one pound sterling, 30 times higher than the usual price.
FACTORY LEFT BEHIND IN TIME
But by 1968, the factory was past its heyday. Its machinery was regarded as old-fashioned and uneconomical and the estate's green tea was sent to other factories for processing.

Instead, it became a warehouse for refuse tea, the fibrous material rejected in the manufacturing process. A few people were employed to sift the fibre and extract any tea for local use. The residue was sold as fertiliser.
The factory finally closed down in 1973.
But Aitken Spence & Co, a leading Sri Lankan business conglomerate with several hotels, had other plans for the rotting pile.

Company officials said they were on the lookout for a suitable tea factory which they could turn into a hotel. The company finally found Hethersett in 1992 and obtained a 99 year lease on it three years later.
The factory was turned into a hotel in 18 months. It cost 150 million rupees ($2.5 million) to create the hotel which opened for its first season last year.
SOME OF THE NOSTALGIA IS INTACT
But while the interior was changed, the original facade and windows and some of the heavy machinery remained in place, if only for nostalgic value.
"There were several tea factories that had closed and we wanted to introduce a unique concept. Mix tourism with tea," said Sridharan.

Once Aitken Spence discovered the place, it reinforced the structure, installed new electrical fittings, reworked the plumbing and converted the withering lofts into bedrooms. They left the original pinewood flooring, which was imported from Sweden in the 1930s, untouched.
The overhead shafts and pulleys, which transferred power using camel hair belts to the machinery, can still be seen on the ground floor of the four-storey building.
In the basement lies the engine that powered the factory, which produced 500 tonnes of top quality tea for the British market every year.
The new owners now plan to add a sauna and turn the nearby manager's house into a conference centre to attract up-market clients.
"We are still not getting the exclusive, high-spending clients, but once everything is in place we should," Sridharan said.
